2024: Community Distributed Generation (CDG, or Community Solar)

A tariff program where a CDG host that installs a DER distributes credits to subscribing customers. Many CDG projects participate in utility consolidated billing (“net crediting”) whereby subscription fees for CDG are collected out of the credit the customer receives. The utility remits these subscription fees, less a 1% admin fee, to the CDG host.
A tariff program whereby a remote crediting host that installs a DER distributes credits to up to 10 accounts associated with the same customer (typically commercial).
A tariff program where a customer installs an eligible DER. Excess net monthly energy credits carry over and are applied against future bills.
2023: Community Distributed Generation (CDG, or Community Solar)

A tariff program where a CDG host that installs a DER distributes credits to subscribing customers. Many CDG projects participate in utility consolidated billing ("net crediting") whereby subscription fees for CDG are collected out of the credit the customer receives. The utility remits these subscription fees, less a 1% admin fee, to the CDG host.
A tariff program where a remote crediting host that installs a DER distributes credit to their own accounts and/or up to 10 customers (typically commercial).
A tariff program where a customer installs an eligible DER. Excess net monthly energy credits carry over and are applied against future bills.

2024: Electric distribution system design utilized by the Company, in which distribution power lines are interconnected in a mesh-like manner. This creates multiple paths for electricity to flow from the source to the load, thereby minimizing the impact of faults. If one line or transformer fails, power supply to customers can be maintained via alternate paths. The network design is predominantly seen in the underground system.

Electric distribution system design utilized by the Company in which power flows in a single path from the source (substation) to the load (customer). If a fault occurs along this path, the affected section loses power until repairs are made. The non-network design is most commonly seen in the radial or overhead system (e.g., power lines on poles).
Any circuit distributing electricity at standard service voltage (120/208 Volts).
Any circuit that delivers power at 4,000, 13,000, 27,000, or 33,000 Volts.
Any operational area in which more than 10% of customers are supplied with electricity via overhead lines.
The loss of service for five minutes or more, for one or more customers, because of one or more electrical component failures.
System Average Interruption Frequency Index, or SAIFI, indicates how many customers experienced an outage in a particular year.
Customer Average Interruption Duration Index, or CAIDI, measures the average time it took the Company to restore power to customers.

Outages that are omitted from the Company’s SAIFI and CAIDI metrics. They are caused by one of the following: - A storm that affects 10% or more of customers in an operating area or when customers in an operating area are out of service for 24 hours or more. - Other events outside of the Company’s control, such as coastal flooding or water main breaks.

Non-excludable outages count against the Company’s SAIFI and CAIDI metrics. Common causes of non-excludable outages include: - Equipment failure (i.e. transformer failure). - Cable failure. - A wire down due to interference from a tree but not related to a storm. - A storm that affects less than 10% of the customers in an operating area, or when customers in an operating area are out of service for fewer than 24 hours.
A device that measures the amount of electric energy consumed by customer equipment

N-2 is a design standard that ensures a system maintains full functionality when up to two major system components fail. In the Company's network design philosophy, N-2 refers to networks that will provide adequate service at peak load with the loss of up to two distribution feeders supplying the network.

N-1 is a design standard that ensures a system maintains full functionality when up to one major system component fails. In the Company's network design philosophy, N-1 refers to networks that will provide adequate service at peak load with the loss of up to one distribution feeder supplying the network

reported.label: Demand-Response Participants
reported.narrative: Total customers enrolled in demand-response programs across CSRP, DLRP, Term-DLM, Auto-DLM, and BYOT.

reported.label: DER Capacity Installed
reported.narrative: Cumulative MW of distributed energy resources interconnected to the distribution system, measured at year-end.

reported.label: Strategic Capital Invested
reported.narrative: Total electric capital investment across environmental, risk-reduction, safety, and system-expansion categories. DAC share is exposure (% affecting DAC areas), not allocated dollars.

reported.label: Outages Interruptions
reported.narrative: Customers interrupted by outages — lower is better. The DAC share signals reliability equity.

reported.label: Leak-Prone Gas Main Replaced
reported.narrative: Linear feet of leak-prone gas main retired and replaced (Bronx + Manhattan + Queens + Westchester). DAC share indicates equitable infrastructure renewal.

reported.label: Gas Leaks Repaired
reported.narrative: Gas leaks repaired across Manhattan, Queens, Westchester, and Bronx. The DAC share captures whether at-risk communities receive equitable response.

reported.label: Clean Energy Job Placements
reported.narrative: Job placements resulting from Con Edison's Clean Energy Academy workforce-development program (unique count).

reported.label: Residential Customers Served
reported.narrative: Total residential customers on the system at year-end. DAC share is the latent demographic baseline against which all program reach should be benchmarked.

analytical.label: DAC Equity Index (Avg DAC %)
analytical.narrative: Simple average of the DAC share across the three dollar-denominated investment KPIs (Clean Energy Incentives · EV Funding · Strategic Capital). Tracks whether equity is improving in aggregate.

analytical.label: Cost per MMBtu Saved
analytical.narrative: Incentive dollars spent per MMBtu of lifetime energy savings achieved. Lower is better — a measure of the program's unit economics.
analytical.source_calc: Section A: total incentive $ ÷ total MMBtu saved

analytical.label: EV Plug Equity Ratio
analytical.narrative: DAC share of EV plug installations divided by the DAC share of residential customers (43.5%). A ratio of 1.0 = parity. Below 1.0 = under-served; above 1.0 = over-indexed (a positive equity outcome).
analytical.source_calc: B2 plugs DAC% ÷ J9 customers DAC%

analytical.label: Outage Burden Ratio
analytical.narrative: DAC share of customers interrupted divided by DAC share of all customers. 1.0 = parity. Below 1.0 = DACs experience proportionally fewer outages (good); above 1.0 = DACs disproportionately impacted.
analytical.source_calc: F7 customers interrupted DAC% ÷ J9 customers DAC%

analytical.label: Leak Repair Equity Ratio
analytical.narrative: DAC share of gas leak repairs divided by DAC share of all customers. Below 1.0 means DACs may be receiving fewer repairs proportionally; above 1.0 means DACs receive a disproportionate share of repair work — likely reflecting older infrastructure but warranting attention.
analytical.source_calc: H1 leak repairs DAC% ÷ J9 customers DAC%

analytical.label: EAP Discount per DAC Customer
analytical.narrative: Average annual EAP (Energy Affordability Program) discount dollars delivered per enrolled customer in disadvantaged communities. Notes: 2023 figure is from a partial year (Apr–Dec) and is not directly comparable.
analytical.source_calc: (J8 DAC electric + gas $) ÷ (J7 DAC electric + gas + dual enrollees)
